metadata.title: Make It Check Its Own Work.
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: show-tell style (Bear, 2026-09-26): opens on the hesitant writer + terms card, no verdict card; Your Turn is the Claude.ai composer; spoken outro stays.

beats.narration_text: Ciao. This is Liam, in for Bear. You ask the AI something, and the answer lands looking confident and complete. So here is the move this film is about: never take the first answer. Make it check its own work.

show.event: types 'The first answer is the final answer.'

props.text:
The first answer
is the final answer.

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the naive take and corrects it to the film's claim: the first answer is a draft.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Three terms for this film. Self-critique: asking the AI to attack its own answer. An assumption: something the answer takes for granted. An objection: the strongest case against it. With those three words, you can run the whole move.

terms.def: asking the AI to find the flaws in its own answer
something the answer takes for granted
the strongest case against the answer

beats.narration_text: The move is one extra message. The AI gives you its answer, and instead of accepting it, you send it back with a job: read this like a critic. A second pair of eyes — even the same pair, looking twice.

shot.visual_intent: A chat window; the answer card lands inside; the critic's magnifier swings over it; a check lands.
shot.motion_claim: A chat window; the answer card lands inside; the critic's magnifier swings over it; a check lands.

beats.narration_text: Here are the three questions that do the work. One: what is wrong with this answer? Two: what did you assume? Three: what is the strongest objection to it? Copy any one of them into your next chat and watch what happens.

shot.visual_intent: Three question cards stack in, one per spoken question.
shot.motion_claim: Three question cards stack in, one per spoken question.

beats.narration_text: Watch it work on a real question. You ask: which months have twenty-eight days? The answer comes back instantly, confident: February. Feels right. It is also wrong.

shot.visual_intent: Twelve month pills; the answer card 'February' lands; the February pill glows; the glow dies into an X.

show.event: answer card 'February' lands; February pill glows
the X lands on the card

shot.motion_claim: Twelve month pills; the answer card 'February' lands; the February pill glows; the glow dies into an X.

beats.narration_text: Now the move. You write back: what is wrong with your answer? The AI re-reads its own words — and catches it. February has twenty-eight days, but so does every other month. The real answer: all of them.

shot.visual_intent: The critique prompt lands; the February glow dies; all twelve pills light in a wave; the card swaps to 'All twelve.'

show.event: all twelve pills light in a wave
answer card swaps to 'All twelve.'; check lands

shot.motion_claim: The critique prompt lands; the February glow dies; all twelve pills light in a wave; the card swaps to 'All twelve.'

beats.narration_text: It works on writing, not just quizzes. You ask for an email to your boss. The draft lands — correct, and quietly rude. One critique later, it spots the tone problem and rewrites it like someone who wants to keep their job.

shot.visual_intent: The email draft lands; 'as I already explained' underlines terracotta; the softened redraft lands; check.

show.event: check lands on the new card

shot.motion_claim: The email draft lands; 'as I already explained' underlines terracotta; the softened redraft lands; check.

beats.narration_text: Spend the second pass where being wrong costs you. Numbers, dates, code, plans — anything you cannot check by eye. A wrong date in a contract beats a wrong fact about penguins. Critique what matters.

shot.visual_intent: Four icon cards — numbers, dates, code, plans — each stamped with a check as named.
shot.motion_claim: Four icon cards — numbers, dates, code, plans — each stamped with a check as named.

beats.narration_text: The honest part. The critic is the same brain that wrote the answer, so it can miss the same blind spots. Worse: it sometimes invents flaws and breaks what was fine. Self-critique cuts errors. It does not delete them. You stay the judge.

shot.visual_intent: The lens passes over a dim crack it never lights; a terracotta patch lands on a fine line; the YOU pill lands.

show.event: lens passes; the crack stays dim
terracotta patch lands on a fine line

shot.motion_claim: The lens passes over a dim crack it never lights; a terracotta patch lands on a fine line; the YOU pill lands.

beats.narration_text: One upgrade. Never ask: is this right? That question only ever gets one answer: yes. Ask what is wrong instead. Give the critic a job — hunting flaws — and it will hunt. A yes-or-no question just gets a nod.

shot.visual_intent: 'Is this right?' earns a YES stamp; 'What's wrong with this?' pops three flaw flags.

show.event: prompt pill 'What's wrong with this?' lands

shot.motion_claim: 'Is this right?' earns a YES stamp; 'What's wrong with this?' pops three flaw flags.

beats.narration_text: So make it a reflex. On anything that matters: get the answer, send it back for a critique, then decide. Two messages instead of one. That is the whole habit.

shot.visual_intent: A loop draws: answer card, arrow, magnifier, arrow, answer card; the three question cards feed in.

show.event: three mini question cards feed the loop

shot.motion_claim: A loop draws: answer card, arrow, magnifier, arrow, answer card; the three question cards feed in.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Read your last answer and be your own toughest critic. List its three weakest points, and tell me what you would change. Run it on something the AI already answered for you — then verify one claim yourself. You are still the judge.
